item.research_question: How does valence electron concentration (VEC) control the fracture resistance and deformation mechanisms of cubic-B1 refractory high-entropy carbides (HECs)?
item.material_system: Six five-cation rocksalt (B1) HECs: (Ti,Zr,Hf,Nb,Ta)C, (Ti,Zr,Hf,Ta,W)C, (Ti,V,Nb,Ta,W)C, (V,Nb,Ta,Mo,W)C, (V,Ta,Cr,Mo,W)C, and (V,Nb,Cr,Mo,W)C, with VEC ranging from 8.4 to 9.6 e−/f.u.
item.processing_route: High-energy ball milling of binary carbides (Cr3C2, HfC, Mo2C, NbC, TaC, TiC, VC, W2C, ZrC) in argon for 2 hours (30-min intervals with 15-min breaks), followed by spark plasma sintering at 2473 K, 30 MPa uniaxial pressure, 100 K/min heating rate, and 10-min dwell under vacuum.
item.test_conditions: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) tensile simulations at 300 K along [001] and [110] directions with 2% strain increments; nanoindentation on polycrystalline samples with loads from 50 to 500 mN and penetration depths up to 1100 nm.
key_findings: HECs with VEC ≤ 9.0 e−/f.u. fracture in a brittle manner at theoretical strengths of ≈26 to 27 GPa and elongations of 10 to 14%.
HECs with VEC ≥ 9.4 e−/f.u. yield at ≈8% strain via transformation-induced plasticity rather than fracturing immediately.
High-VEC alloys withstand [001] elongations of 22, 28, and 30% before rupture, compared to 10–14% for low-VEC alloys.
At 50 mN load and 200 nm penetration, low-VEC alloys fracture in ≈20 ± 10% of tests, while high-VEC alloys fracture in only ≈0 to 3%.
At severe conditions (300 mN load, 600 nm penetration), low-VEC alloys fracture in nearly 100% of tests, whereas high-VEC alloys resist fracture in 30 to 60% of tests.
Theoretical tensile toughness (UT) increases superlinearly for VEC > 8.5 e−/f.u., while hardness remains in the range of 27 to 33 GPa for all compositions.
Electron rehybridization in high-VEC alloys facilitates the redistribution of electrons into d-d bonds between next-nearest-neighbor metal atoms during strain.
item.mechanism: A high VEC (≳ 9.4 e−/f.u.) enhances fracture resistance by enabling facile rehybridization of electronic metallic states near the Fermi level, which activates transformation plasticity. This allows the material to redistribute electrons into d-d bonds between next-nearest-neighbor metal atoms, modifying bond angles and atomic coordination to dissipate stress and delay rupture, rather than failing via brittle cleavage.
item.limitations: The study notes that AIMD simulations use defect-free single-crystal models and high strain rates, yielding ideal upper bounds for strength and elongation that exceed experimental values. Additionally, the presence of native defects (dislocations, grain boundaries), point defects, and stacking faults in real bulk materials causes deviations from the theoretical trends predicted for defect-free crystals.
item.future_work: The authors propose conducting in-depth transmission electron microscopy to locate stress-induced nanoscale transformations, investigating long-term durability under thermal cycling and oxidation, and performing larger-scale atomistic simulations (nm3 to µm3) using machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to account for native defects and quantitatively evaluate fracture toughness (KIc).
quotes: VEC ≳ 9.4 electrons per formula unit enhances alloy fracture resistance due to a facile rehybridization of electronic metallic states, which activates transformation plasticity at the yield point.
The ability of high-VEC HECs to redistribute electrons during deformation enables transformation plasticity, which enhances the material resistance to fracture at a low expense in hardness.
